references.text: In Matthew's account of the crucifixion, the inscription above Jesus' head is also mentioned: "This is Jesus, the King of the Jews" ([ref:Matt 27:37|Matthew 27:37]). All four gospels mention this inscription, but with slight variations in wording.
Mark reports that the inscription accusing Jesus read: "The King of the Jews" ([ref:Mark 15:26|Mark 15:26]). This is the shortest version of the inscription among the gospels.

John gives the most detailed account of the inscription. Pilate wrote, "Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews," and it was written in Hebrew, Latin, and Greek. The chief priests protested, but Pilate answered: "What I have written, I have written" ([ref:Joh 19:19-22|John 19:19-22]).

During the trial, Pilate asked Jesus: "Are you the King of the Jews?" The title "King of the Jews," used in the inscription, reflects exactly this charge brought against Jesus ([ref:Luk 23:3|Luke 23:3]).
The charge against Jesus before Pilate was that he claimed to be Christ, a king. The inscription on the cross summarized this accusation ([ref:Luk 23:2|Luke 23:2]).

Already at Jesus' birth, the title "King of the Jews" was used by the wise men from the East: "Where is he who has been born King of the Jews?" ([ref:Matt 2:2|Matthew 2:2]). The inscription on the cross stands in ironic contrast to this royal title.

Just before the mention of the inscription, the soldiers mock Jesus and say: "If you are the King of the Jews, save yourself!" ([ref:Luk 23:37|Luke 23:37]). The inscription underscores the charge that formed the basis for both mockery and judgment.

In the conversation between Pilate and Jesus, Jesus' kingdom is discussed. Jesus confirms that he is a king, but that his kingdom is not of this world ([ref:Joh 18:33-37|John 18:33-37]). The inscription on the cross points back to this trial.
